title: Judges 20:29–48
context: On the third day Israel sets an ambush, draws Benjamin away from Gibeah, and the city is struck and burned. The LORD strikes Benjamin before Israel, and the tribe is almost wiped out: only six hundred men escape to the rock of Rimmon, while the Israelites go on to destroy Benjamin’s towns, livestock and people. The figures given in different verses do not add up in an obvious way, and interpreters explain them differently. Readers in both traditions commonly read this section as just judgment on Gibeah’s crime and Benjamin’s refusal to give up the guilty, carried out with a destructive excess that the narrative does not commend. The near-loss of a whole tribe is presented as a tragedy, as chapter 21 makes clear.

verses.text: Israel set ambushes all around Gibeah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Israel setting ambushes around Gibeah, a new strategy for the third day. Human planning and God’s promise operate together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s promised victory being carried out through ordinary means of strategy. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing God working through human action.

verses.text: The children of Israel went up against the children of Benjamin on the third day, and set themselves in array against Gibeah, as at other times.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Israel arraying against Gibeah as at other times. The familiar pattern sets up the surprise of the ambush.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repetition as part of the narrative’s design. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as preparing for the reversal that follows.

verses.text: The children of Benjamin went out against the people, and were drawn away from the city; and they began to strike and kill of the people as at other times, in the highways, of which one goes up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah, in the field, about thirty men of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Benjamin drawn away from the city and killing about thirty Israelites on the highways. The pattern seems to repeat the earlier days.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Benjamin’s early success is part of Israel’s plan. Both traditions commonly hold the locations of the highways with the caution appropriate to ancient geography.

verses.text: The children of Benjamin said, “They are struck down before us, as at the first.” But the children of Israel said, “Let’s flee, and draw them away from the city to the highways.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Benjamin’s confidence that Israel is defeated as before. Their overconfidence, built on two earlier victories, blinds them to the trap.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the narrative irony as Israel feigns retreat. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing the danger of trusting past success.

verses.text: All the men of Israel rose up out of their place and set themselves in array at Baal Tamar. Then the ambushers of Israel broke out of their place, even out of Maareh Geba.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the ambush breaking out at Maareh Geba as Israel regroups at Baal Tamar. The exact locations are uncertain, but the strategy is clear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the place names with caution while following the movement of the battle. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the turning point of the conflict.

verses.text: Ten thousand chosen men out of all Israel came over against Gibeah, and the battle was severe; but they didn’t know that disaster was close to them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the battle was severe and that Benjamin did not know disaster was near. Judgment can come suddenly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the hidden approach of disaster as part of God’s promised deliverance of Benjamin into Israel’s hand. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, as the beginning of a terrible loss.

verses.text: The LORD struck Benjamin before Israel; and the children of Israel destroyed of Benjamin that day twenty-five thousand one hundred men. All these drew the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the statement that the LORD struck Benjamin before Israel. The victory is attributed to God, fulfilling the promise of verse 28.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign action in the outcome of the battle. Both traditions commonly affirm God’s involvement while noting that this does not endorse every act of destruction that follows.

verses.text: So the children of Benjamin saw that they were struck, for the men of Israel yielded to Benjamin because they trusted the ambushers whom they had set against Gibeah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the explanation that Israel yielded ground because they trusted the ambushers. The narrative retells the battle from a different angle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repetition as typical of Hebrew narrative, which sometimes recounts events more than once. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as clarifying the strategy.

verses.text: The ambushers hurried, and rushed on Gibeah; then the ambushers spread out, and struck all the city with the edge of the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the ambushers rushing on Gibeah and striking the city. The town at the center of the crime against the woman now falls.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see judgment falling on Gibeah, though the extent of destruction raises sober questions. Both traditions commonly read the verse as reporting what happened rather than commending every detail.

verses.text: Now the appointed sign between the men of Israel and the ambushers was that they should make a great cloud of smoke rise up out of the city.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the agreed signal of a great cloud of smoke rising from the city. Careful coordination between the two forces makes the plan work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the signal as part of the careful execution of the strategy. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as narrative detail without further doctrinal weight.

verses.text: The men of Israel turned in the battle, and Benjamin began to strike and kill of the men of Israel about thirty persons; for they said, “Surely they are struck down before us, as in the first battle.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Israel turning in battle while Benjamin still thinks it is winning. Perception and reality are far apart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Benjamin’s false confidence as part of the narrative’s irony. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing how quickly fortunes can reverse.

verses.text: But when the cloud began to arise up out of the city in a pillar of smoke, the Benjamites looked behind them; and behold, the whole city went up in smoke to the sky.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Benjamin looking back to see the whole city going up in smoke. The moment of realization is devastating.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the burning of Gibeah as the visible sign of judgment on the town. Readers in both traditions commonly read the image soberly, mindful of the cost of the war.

verses.text: The men of Israel turned, and the men of Benjamin were dismayed; for they saw that disaster had come on them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the men of Benjamin dismayed when they realize disaster has come. Their earlier refusal to give up the guilty now brings ruin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the consequence of siding with wrongdoers. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a tragic outcome of Benjamin’s choice in verse 13.

verses.text: Therefore they turned their backs before the men of Israel to the way of the wilderness, but the battle followed hard after them; and those who came out of the cities destroyed them in the middle of it.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Benjamin fleeing toward the wilderness while the battle follows hard. Escape seems impossible as the pursuit closes in from several directions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the pursuit as part of the overwhelming defeat. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse with sorrow at the scale of the loss among fellow Israelites.

verses.text: They surrounded the Benjamites, chased them, and trod them down at their resting place, as far as near Gibeah toward the sunrise.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Benjamites surrounded and trodden down. The vivid language conveys the thoroughness and severity of the defeat.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the narrative’s vivid portrayal of the rout. Both traditions commonly read it as reporting a grim reality, not celebrating it.

verses.text: Eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fell; all these were men of valor.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fell, all men of valor. The narrator acknowledges their courage even in defeat.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the description as recognizing the human cost on both sides. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the tragedy of civil war.

verses.text: They turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon. They gleaned five thousand men of them in the highways, and followed hard after them to Gidom, and struck two thousand men of them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the pursuit continuing toward the rock of Rimmon, with thousands more struck down. The exact places named are uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the locations with caution while noting the relentless pursuit. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing how the conflict escalated beyond punishing the guilty.

verses.text: So that all who fell that day of Benjamin were twenty-five thousand men who drew the sword. All these were men of valor.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the total of twenty-five thousand Benjamites who fell. The figures in this chapter do not add up in an obvious way, and interpreters explain the differences variously.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the numbers with care while affirming the scale of the loss. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as summarizing a catastrophe for one of Israel’s tribes.

verses.text: But six hundred men turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon, and stayed in the rock of Rimmon four months.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the six hundred men who escaped to the rock of Rimmon and stayed there four months. A small remnant of the tribe survives the catastrophe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the preservation of a remnant as setting up the efforts to restore Benjamin in chapter 21. Both traditions commonly find a faint note of hope amid the devastation.

verses.text: The men of Israel turned again on the children of Benjamin, and struck them with the edge of the sword—including the entire city, the livestock, and all that they found. Moreover they set all the cities which they found on fire.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Israel turning on Benjamin’s towns, livestock and people and burning the cities. The destruction goes far beyond the guilty men of Gibeah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the excess of this violence, which the narrator reports without commendation. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing how justice can turn into vengeance when restraint is lost (compare Romans 12:19).
